ideas.title: Night Golf
ideas.oneLiner: Glowing balls, lit greens and neon course features that let courses run fun, party-atmosphere golf after dark — unlocking off-peak evening revenue.

market.why: US golf is in a genuine boom — ~16,000 courses at 14,000 facilities, 28M on-course golfers in 2024 and 48M total participants in 2025, up 41% since 2019, with new-course development at its highest since 2011. Experiential and off-course formats (incl. night play) are the growth edge, and 100+ lit courses were in development as of early 2025. The specific 'night golf' spend is still a niche slice of that — sizing it precisely is the open question.

entry.why: Low barriers on the lean path: glow gear is a commodity you can source cheaply, portable LED event kits are inexpensive, and there's no regulation. You can launch as a mobile night-golf events service in one region for a few thousand dollars. (Permanently lighting courses is the high-barrier version — avoid early.)

cost.why: Cheap to first revenue if you run mobile events / sell self-run kits: a few thousand dollars of portable LED gear plus glow inventory, and you can book paid event nights quickly. Costs balloon only if you pursue permanent course lighting ($5,000–$20,000 per light, six figures per course).

saturation.why: The weak spot. Glow-in-the-dark golf balls are a heavily commoditised category (Premier Glow, Crestgolf, Sundown, THIODOON, plus Amazon/Walmart/Dick's) at $14–40 a pack. The experiential-events angle is more open but already has a scaled leader — Glow Vibe Golf has run 1,500+ events across 36 states since 2014.

moat.why: Inherently low. The gear is commodity and events are replicable. Thin defensibility is possible via brand, exclusive course contracts/territories, or a productised self-serve kit with recurring consumables — but nothing structurally protects it.

margins.why: Mixed. Commodity consumables (glow balls, markers) are low-margin but recurring; staffed experiences and event bookings carry higher service margins. Blended margin is moderate and scales through a kit/franchise model rather than manufacturing.

founderFit.why: Good fit for a sourcing-and-marketing-led experiential product: the team brings overseas manufacturing/sourcing access (low-cost glow gear), strong experiential-marketing and sports/events instinct, product engineering, and B2B/finance skills for selling to course operators. The gap: no golf-industry insiders or existing course relationships, which matters for B2B adoption.

risk.why: Moderate. Headwinds: a scaled incumbent, commodity/low-moat economics, outdoor seasonality and weather, and dependence on relatively conservative course operators choosing to adopt. Upside: capital-at-risk is low on the lean path, so the downside is contained.

businessCase.summary: Night Golf turns unused after-dark hours into a fun, party-atmosphere revenue stream for golf courses. There are two layers: a commodity glow-gear product (saturated, weak) and the real opportunity — a turnkey experiential night-golf offering (events + a self-run kit) that helps the ~16,000 US courses monetise off-peak evenings and reach the fast-growing experience-seeking crowd. Demand is rising, but an established leader (Glow Vibe Golf) is already scaling it, so this is a fast-follower play, not a blue ocean.
businessCase.customer: Two-sided. The paying B2B buyer is the golf-course / driving-range operator — especially public, municipal and resort courses chasing off-peak and event revenue. The end users are casual and social golfers, corporate outings, charity fundraisers, date-night/party groups, and juniors — the fastest-growing, experience-led segments of the game.
businessCase.market: US golf is booming: ~16,000 courses / 14,000 facilities, on-course golfers up to 28M (2024) and 48M total participants (2025), +41% since 2019, with course development at a post-2011 high and record-low closures. Experiential and night formats are a growth edge (100+ lit courses in development in early 2025). The night-golf sub-segment specifically is a niche of that whole — real TAM sizing is the key unknown (flagged low-confidence).
businessCase.model: Layered revenue: (1) mobile, turnkey glow-golf event nights sold per-event to courses (the proven Glow Vibe model); (2) a 'night-golf-in-a-box' kit sold or leased to courses so they self-run events, generating upfront hardware plus recurring consumables (glow balls, markers, cart lights); (3) recurring replenishment revenue on those consumables; optionally (4) higher-tier permanent lighting installs later (capital-heavy).
businessCase.goToMarket: Land regional courses with a couple of paid pilot event nights, then convert them to a recurring kit + consumables relationship. Lean hard on experiential/social marketing — glow-golf content is highly shareable — and target high-value corporate outings and charity fundraisers. Expand territory by territory, prioritising areas the incumbent doesn't cover.
businessCase.costs: Lean path is cheap: a few thousand dollars of portable LED gear and glow inventory (cheaply sourced overseas) to run the first events. Ongoing costs are inventory, event staffing/labour and logistics. The expensive path — permanently lighting courses at $5k–$20k per light — should be avoided until demand is proven.
businessCase.risks: A scaled competitor (Glow Vibe Golf) already owns the experiential niche; the gear is a commodity with weak defensibility; outdoor play is weather- and season-dependent; and success hinges on conservative course operators adopting. The literal 'manufacture and sell glow balls' interpretation is a race to the bottom and should be avoided.
businessCase.nextSteps: 1) Decide the layer — events/kit for courses, NOT manufacturing balls. 2) Run 2–3 paid pilot nights with local courses to test willingness-to-pay and rebooking. 3) Price a self-serve kit + consumables model. 4) Map where Glow Vibe Golf is absent. 5) Validate the overseas-sourced gear cost advantage.

clarifyingQuestions: Which layer are we actually building — the commodity glow-ball product, staffed mobile events, or a self-serve 'night-golf kit + consumables' for courses? They're very different businesses.
Is the paying customer the golf course (B2B) or the end golfer (B2C), and where does the recurring revenue come from?
How do we differentiate from Glow Vibe Golf, who already run 1,500+ night-golf events across 36 states?
Do any of us have relationships with golf courses or operators we could use to land the first pilots?
